It is a great pleasure to welcome you to Little Ilford School
We hope you enjoy browsing our website and find it informative and will give you a good perspective of our aims. Little Ilford School is a ‘Good’ school with strong values and a clear vision. We offer a well-balanced curriculum with a wide range of extracurricular opportunities. We have high expectations of our students and encourage them to reflect the school values of ‘Courage, Commitment and Compassion’ and live by our school vision ‘We take ownership of our learning and aspirations so that we fulfil our unique potential.’ We want students to be happy, aim high, be lifelong learners, and be responsible role models. Our aims are further supported by our status as a Leading Edge School; we take a focused approach in the professional development of teachers and support staff, striving to raise our standards and fully support every member of our community. If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to contact us. Jenny Evans

Little Ilford School would welcome you applying for a place at our school
Little Ilford School offers a well-structured and transparent admissions process designed to support students and families at every stage of entry. As a popular and inclusive secondary school, admissions are coordinated in line with local authority guidelines, ensuring fairness and equal opportunity for all applicants. Prospective students typically join the school in Year 7 through the coordinated admissions process managed by the local council. Parents and carers are encouraged to apply within the specified deadlines and to carefully review the published admissions criteria, which outline how places are allocated when applications exceed available spaces. The school welcomes applications from families both within and outside the local area.

Welcome
Welcome to Little Ilford School
It is a privilege to welcome you to Little Ilford School. Having served this community for over five years as Deputy Headteacher and now leading the school as interim Headteacher, I am immensely proud of our dedicated staff, our vibrant community, and—above all—our students.
Little Ilford is an inclusive, values-driven school with a clear purpose. We offer a well-balanced, ambitious curriculum paired with a rich extra-curricular programme, encouraging every student to embody our core values of Courage, Commitment, and Compassion. We set high expectations and challenge our students every day to take ownership of their learning, strive to be better today than they were yesterday, and realise their unique potential.
As a Leading Edge school, we invest continuously in the professional development of our staff. This ensures we deliver high-quality teaching within a safe, supportive, and structured environment where every child can flourish.
Whether you are a current family, a prospective parent/carer, or a visitor, we hope our website gives you a clear sense of our culture and aspirations. Please do not hesitate to contact us if you would like to find out more.
Headteacher (Interim)

The Story Behind Our Logo
The scholar at the heart of the Little Ilford School logo is Thomas Heron, the eldest son of Sir John Heron—Private Treasurer to Henry VIII and Lord of the Manor of Aldersbrook.
Our school badge features a drawing of Thomas adapted from a 500-year-old brass memorial located at St Mary’s Church in our local community. Hanging from his belt are an inkhorn and pencase, signalling his status as a scholar. As one of only three surviving Tudor brasses of its kind in the entire United Kingdom, Thomas Heron’s memorial represents a remarkable local legacy—one that our students wear with pride every day.

About us
Courage, Commitment, Compassion
Founded in 1957, Little Ilford School is a successful mixed multicultural 11-16 secondary school with 12 forms of entry situated in the London Borough of Newham.
We are a high achieving school and proud of our diverse and celebratory institution that enjoys an excellent reputation and strives to be an outward facing school working closely with our community.
We are culturally rich with an ethos based around praise, support and caring for each other. We have very high aspirations for the students whatever their personal or social challenges; we systematically remove all barriers to learning to ensure that all of our students can fulfil their potential and leave us as fully active citizens of the Manor Park community.
Most of our students begin at LIS well below national standards but achieve in line with, or exceed, national standards when they leave in Year 11; our students achieve well above national rates of progression. We expect all of our students to excel.
We intend to ensure that our students achieve even higher rates of progress and outcomes through high quality learning and teaching and a curriculum that provides opportunities for all students to excel.

Alternative pathways at KS4
We offer a level 1 qualification called the Drama Entry Pathway accredited by WJEC.
This is not a GCSE but students can accumulate credits for a range of skills - voice, movement, creating an original piece and performing as part of a group.
This can be taught alongside the GCSE and may suit some students better than the GCSE.
ASDAN Expressive Arts
We also offer ASDAN Expressive Arts to students on the course with significant SEN if they will not be able to complete the written examination for GCSE. This requires the students to work on a group project for an extended amount of time and runs in partnership with the GCSE Component 1 unit.
We offer an extensive enrichment and extracurricular curriculum alongside formal lessons.
Students have an opportunity to perform for an audience at the end of every term. This includes a whole school play, open to all in the Autumn Term.
We organise theatre visits at regular intervals for GCSE students, both for their GCSE course and a Saturday Matinee club where we book 20 tickets to different performances throughout the year in different venues which are offered on a first come, first served basis for students studying GCSE Drama. These trips are to venues such as The Young Vic, The Old Vic, The Donmar Warehouse, The National Theatre (Olivier, Lyttleton and Dorfman) Soho Theatre, Sadlers Wells and Theatre Royal Stratford East. These trips take place usually in the evening or on Saturdays to avoid missing learning time.
We have also started to take selected students in year 8 and 9 to the theatre as a praise reward visit for their hard work in drama lessons.
We have links with organisations such as Frantic Assembly, The Donmar Warehouse and English National Ballet (Sadlers Wells) as well as professional actors and directors who come in to lead workshops in school so that our students can extend their understanding as well as work with industry professionals.
Home learning
Year 7 and 8
Students will be expected to complete regular home learning tasks. These will be set on Google Classroom.
These will include: learning lines for performance, self assessments and target setting, answering key philosophical questions, lighting design, costume design and some research into practitioners or rehearsal techniques.
Year 9
Students will be expected to complete regular home learning including tasks building on the skills learnt in years 7 and 8 including: in-depth research into different practitioners and artists (Frantic Assembly, Stanislavski, Brecht, Lemn Sissay, Warsan Shire) lighting design, set design, costume, hair and make up design, workshop planning and evaluation.
KS4 (years 10 and 11)
As further development of the skills learnt in KS3, students will be expected to complete regular home learning tasks such as: learning lines for entire scenes from plays, written logs for practitioner workshops and practical devising lessons, answering exam style questions in the key areas of lighting design, set design, costume, hair and make-up design, directing and acting.
As well as this they will be required to do independent research into the themes and issues we explore in lessons. This is particularly the case in year 10 and 11. (Comp 1 Devising Ideas)
They will be expected to learn lines for practical assessments. (Comp 2 Performance from Text)
All the resources they will need to access will be available on Google Classroom.
How parents/carers can support their child
Taking an interest in what your child is doing, asking them to tell you what their work was like. Share what is being completed and recorded on Google Classroom. Give them access to high quality acting (not Eastenders) and take them to the theatre whenever possible.

SEND Provision at Little Ilford School
The Special Educational Needs and Disabilities Team (SEND) team comprises staff with a range of skills and knowledge. The SEND team works collaboratively with pastoral teams and the behaviour support team to develop an inclusive approach to learning. Externally, the SEND team maintains strong and productive relationships with the London Borough of Newham SEN Department as well as with its specialist services. These include the Newham Sensory Service, Newham Language Communication and Interaction Service (LCIS), the Newham Educational Psychology Service, the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS), the NHS and other external agencies. We seek at all times to provide the best possible holistic support for students. The team oversees Medical Care Plans and Exam Access Arrangements.
Levels of need are categorised under four main headings:
Communication and Interaction
Cognition and Learning
Social, Emotional and Mental Health Difficulties
Sensory and/or Physical Needs
Primary to Secondary Transition
To support the secondary transition process, the SEN team attends Transfer Reviews for students with EHC plans in the Summer Term prior to the student’s admission. This helps to ensure a smooth transition from Key Stage 2. Where possible the SEN team will visit year 6 students in their setting to support transition further. When required, students who need further support with transition will be invited to attend the school in the summer term.

Overview
ASDAN programs of study can support the delivery of a balanced, broad and relevant curriculum. They are of benefit to the students within the school, equipping them with skills and processes that will benefit them across the curriculum and later into adult life. The programs of study provide students with those personal and social skills as well as transferable educational skills that can aid them throughout the school curriculum and later life. ASDAN creates opportunities for all students to achieve, regardless of the barriers to learning. The PSD course enables learners to gain skills with personal and social development through their achievements, thereby enhancing self-confidence, ambition and contribution to their communities. It also provides transferable skills that students can apply and use across the curriculum.
Teaching Aims
The ASDAN curriculum is designed to
The ASDAN Level 1 Award in Personal and Social Development incorporates aspects of personal, social, health, citizenship and ICT, and enables candidates to develop skills that prepare them for independence and working life. It offers imaginative ways of supporting young people in becoming confident individuals who are physically, emotionally and socially healthy, being responsible citizens who make a positive contribution to society and embrace change, managing risk together with their own wellbeing, as well as introducing them to new activities and personal challenges.

Accessibility & Inclusion
STEP UP
Step Up is a specialised, non-exam-based course tailored specifically for students who require further, significant intervention to access the English curriculum beyond standard GCSE lessons. It is designed for students who we anticipate may not achieve a formal grade at GCSE level, providing them with a meaningful and accessible pathway to success.
Because the course is designed for students with varying needs, teachers can choose from a range of engaging, themed units (such as "Holidays" or "Pets") to select topics that best capture individual interest. Students are entered for either the Silver or Gold step, depending on their current academic level, allowing them to work and progress at a pace that perfectly suits their personal development.
Study Plus:
Study Plus as an Option Subject
Designed specifically for our Year 10 and 11 GCSE students, Study Plus is a targeted option subject that provides six additional, dedicated sessions focused entirely on maximising English potential. By operating in smaller class sizes with a scaled-down, highly focused curriculum, Study Plus creates a supportive environment where students can truly build their confidence and expertise. The programme delivers targeted intervention by systematically revising core topics covered in regular English lessons, providing structured revision time, and embedding vital exam skills practice. It is the ideal choice for students looking to reinforce their classroom learning, sharpen their exam techniques, and approach their final assessments with total confidence.
English Language and English Literature GCSEs
Supportive Classrooms and Collaborative Learning. We keep our English classes capped at a maximum of 24 students. These smaller numbers mean teachers can move around the room easily, giving your child frequent, one-on-one feedback and helping them the moment they get stuck. In these classrooms, students of all abilities learn together. Through structured group activities—like partnering up to discuss ideas before writing them down—students naturally support one another. Stronger readers help model high-level vocabulary, which takes the pressure off students who find the subject more challenging or speak English as an additional language.
Fairness in Exam Design and Support.
Preparing for GCSE Success
Because GCSE English is untiered—meaning every student sits the exact same exam paper and has the opportunity to achieve the highest grades (1 to 9)—we design our lessons to ensure no student is capped in their potential, while providing robust support so everyone can access the curriculum.
Here is how we adapt our teaching to prepare all students for GCSE success:
Teaching to the Top, Scaffolding Down: We introduce high-level, sophisticated ideas and vocabulary to the whole class, and then use targeted support—such as sentence stems, analytical templates, and key-term banks—to help every student reach those high standards.
Deconstructing Exam Questions: We break down complex, multi-step exam questions into simple, memorable routines. Students learn exactly "what" the question is looking for and "how" to plan their time before they start writing.
Building Exam Stamina Gradually: Sitting a long English exam can be daunting. We build student stamina progressively over time, starting with focused single-paragraph responses under timed conditions before moving on to full-length practice essays.
Step-by-Step Modeling: Before asking students to write independently under exam conditions, teachers live-model the writing process on the board, demonstrating how to plan, draft, and self-correct work in real time.
Targeted Feedback & Reflection Time: We use regular, low-stakes exam practice to pinpoint exactly where students are making progress or hitting barriers, allowing us to immediately adapt our next lessons to address any gaps in understanding.
Everyday Learning Tools and Guides
We use practical, in-lesson support and targeted interventions to ensure complex texts and writing tasks never feel overwhelming. Here are the core strategies our teachers use in every English lesson to support all learners:
Knowledge Organisers: At the start of every topic, students receive a Knowledge Organiser. This single-page reference sheet maps out the "bigger picture"—including key plot points, historical context, famous quotes, and essential vocabulary—to reduce cognitive load and boost confidence.
Visual Mapping & Dual-Coding: We match complex words with visual pictures, timelines, and graphic organisers. This helps students visually map out complex plots, like Scrooge’s journey in A Christmas Carol or the sequence of events in Macbeth.
Chunking: We break down lengthy texts and complex writing tasks into smaller, manageable "chunks" so students can focus on mastering one step at a time.
Scaffolded Extended Writing: We don’t expect students to face a blank page alone. We provide writing scaffolds, such as sentence starters, paragraph templates, and word banks, to help them confidently turn their spoken ideas into well-structured, independent essays.
Use of WAGOLL (What A Good One Looks Like): Teachers share high-quality, pre-written model answers. This gives students a clear blueprint of what success looks like before they pick up their pens.
Explicit Vocabulary & The Frayer Model: To teach challenging Tier 3 (academic and subject-specific) language, we use the Frayer Model. This four-part graphic organiser helps students break down a word by its definition, characteristics, examples, and non-examples, ensuring they deeply understand the word rather than just memorising it.
Supported Reading Lessons: To ensure reading is accessible to everyone, we adapt our lessons by pre-teaching key vocabulary, reading texts aloud as a class, and providing structured guided reading booklets to keep all students on track.
Home learning (frequency and expectations)
Teachers set homework on a weekly basis using Google classroom. We aim to create independent learners through the use of additional reading, revision and resources on Google classroom. Students may be asked to undertake any of the following: learning spellings and quotations, quizzes, grammar exercises, knowledge tests, creating knowledge organisers and revision resources, taking practice papers, GCSE questions and project-based research. Home learning is used to encourage a cohesive and collaborative learning culture.
Additional Requirements
To improve your English, you are expected to read regularly and actively use the wealth of reading material available in our library. Students at LIS are fortunate to be able to borrow up to six texts. We provide a variety of enrichment activities, from opportunities to see plays in and out of school, working with professional writers and poets and revision-based ‘Glitter’ sessions.

Assessment Component: Demonstrate a sustained commitment to physical activity by fully engaging in mandatory curricular PE (100 minutes per week) and independently tracking and managing additional movement to meet long-term health guidelines.
Accessibility & Inclusion
In Physical Education, we are committed to an “active culture" that ensures inclusion, health, and excellence for every student, regardless of their starting point. To make our curriculum fully accessible, we use a multi-tiered approach to adaptation:
Home learning (frequency and expectations)
Students are expected to spend around two hours per week outside of lesson time completing home learning for the theoretical examinations.
For the practical performance, students are encouraged to be regular sports performers outside of school - this could be at a local sports club, for a sports team, or from making use of the extensive extra-curricular clubs organised by the PE department.
How parents / carers can support their child
This can be achieved through parents being willing to support their child in joining a local sports club, playing fixtures, attending club practise and encouraging them to develop a love for sport and exercise.
While it is an accepted practice that children and youth should be doing homework on a regular basis, the same sentiment is not always transferred to the physical activity area. Yet growth and development in this area are crucial for the well-being and health of the child. When children play, parents often let them do so by themselves. A valuable routine for children, youth, parents and caregivers would be to target some time each day to spend together being physically active. Parents play an integral part in the development of positive attitudes towards physical activity in their children.
For theory lessons and homework, parents can support their child in completing homework that is individualised for each student. This will challenge them as much as possible with support provided for students where the teacher sees necessary.

Our Vision
“To build a better future for myself by becoming a responsible, respectful and active citizen and making positive decisions about my wellbeing.”
How will I do this?
What is RSHE about?
1. Relationships Education
Learning how to build and maintain healthy, respectful, and happy relationships, both offline and online. This focuses heavily on the skills of communication, kindness, and understanding and setting healthy personal boundaries.
2. Sex Education
Learning the factual and legal realities of sex, sexuality, sexual health, and gender reassignment. In line with current guidance, schools present the legal framework (such as the Equality Act) and biological facts, while remaining mindful of ongoing public debates and ensuring they do not teach contested views on gender identity as undisputed facts.
3. Health Education
Learning how to keep fit and healthy, manage physical and mental wellbeing, and navigate modern health challenges. This includes updated content on:
Physical fitness and healthy relationships with food.
